Daylight saving time (DST) has multiple "firsts" depending on scope. The world's first DST period began on July 1, 1908, when residents of Port Arthur, Ontario (today's Thunder Bay), Canada turned their clocks forward by one hour [d3]. At the national level, Germany and Austria were the first countries to adopt DST, setting clocks ahead one hour on April 30, 1916, during World War I to save fuel for the war effort, with the United Kingdom, France, and others soon following [d3][d9][d1]. In the United States, DST was first enacted federally on March 19, 1918, when President Woodrow Wilson signed the Standard Time Act into law, also motivated by wartime fuel conservation [d7][d8][d5]. DST became a permanent federal standard in the US with the Uniform Time Act of 1966, signed by President Lyndon Johnson [d4][d2].
